Article.ArticleTitle: Trend analysis in hand hygiene from the early COVID pandemic to the post-COVID periods at a Tunisian University Hospital.

Abstract.AbstractText: The COVID-19 pandemic has further underscored the importance of Hand Hygiene (HH) adherence as an effective measure for infection prevention and control. This study aims to evaluate trends in HH practices from 2020 to 2023 and assess the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic at the University Hospital of Mahdia (Tunisia).

From June 2020 to October 2023, annual direct observations of HH were performed among health care workers (HCWs) at Mahdia hospital based on the ''HygMain Hygiene audit'' validated by the Practice Assessment Group of Hospital Hygiene in France. Data were collected through structured observations by trained doctors and hygienists. Compliance and relevance rates were analyzed for each observation period.

A total of 993 HH opportunities were observed across five periods from 2020 to 2023, involving 731 HCWs, predominantly paramedical staff (54.4%). Among them, 478 (65%) were female. The overall HH compliance was 22.1%, with a higher compliance rate after patient contact (28.4% vs 39%, p = 0.08). Overall, HH compliance increased significantly during the COVID-19 pandemic, peaking at 33.1% in 2022 before declining to 14.7% in 2023. Similarly, the overall HH relevance rates rose from 6.5% in 2020 to 30% in 2022, but fell to 19.4% in 2023. Compliance was higher in high-risk departments and during invasive procedures.

The study highlights the positive impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on HH, though the post-pandemic adherence rate has declined. Continuous monitoring and institutional support are essential to enhance and maintain compliance levels, ensuring long-term improvements in infection control practices.

Article.ArticleTitle: Sex Differences in the Prevalence, Medical Therapy, and Outcomes in Heart Failure With Improved Ejection Fraction.

Abstract.AbstractText: Heart failure with improved ejection fraction (HFimpEF) is a rapidly growing clinical entity. There is little understanding of how sex relates to the epidemiology, predictors, and trajectory of HFimpEF.

The authors aimed to describe sex-based differences in the epidemiology, guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) use, and clinical outcomes among patients with HFimpEF within a large, diverse health care system.

The authors identified adults with incident heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) (ejection fraction ≤40%) between 2013 and 2022. HFimpEF was defined as a subsequent ejection fraction measurement >40% within the following 12 months. Sex was based on self-report. Among patients with HFimpEF, the authors examined GDMT use at the time of incident HFrEF, HFimpEF, and 1 year following HFimpEF, stratified by sex. They examined the incidence of worsening heart failure (WHF) events and all-cause death 1 year postincident HFrEF. We compared event rates between patients with HFimpEF and persistent HFrEF, adjusted for demographic and clinical characteristics.

Among 28,292 patients with incident HFrEF (females: 34.8%), 35.2% experienced HFimpEF. Females were more likely to experience HFimpEF in the 12 months following HFrEF than males (36.5% vs 34.5%, P < 0.0001). Among patients with HFimpEF, GDMT use was similar among females and males and declined after incident HFimpEF in both sexes. Compared with patients with persistent HFrEF, patients with HFimpEF had better WHF outcomes and all-cause death outcomes, which was consistent by sex. However, females with HFimpEF had higher rates of WHF compared with males with HFimpEF, even when adjusted for clinical covariates.
HFimpEF is associated with improved outcomes for both females and males. However, females with HFimpEF have higher rates of WHF events compared with males.

Article.ArticleTitle: Are Current Lipid Guidelines Adequate for South Asian Patients? A Narrative Review.

Abstract.AbstractText: South Asians, who account for nearly one quarter of the world's population, experience a disproportionately high burden of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), often presenting 5-10 years earlier than European populations. This review evaluates whether contemporary lipid-management frameworks adequately address cardiovascular risk in South Asians. South Asians exhibit a distinct lipid phenotype characterised by elevated apolipoprotein B (ApoB), hypertriglyceridaemia, reduced HDL-cholesterol (HDL-C), increased small dense LDL (sdLDL) particles, and a high prevalence of elevated lipoprotein(a) (Lp(a)), features that are incompletely captured by conventional LDL-cholesterol (LDL-C)-based approaches. Existing cardiovascular risk tools show variable performance in South Asian populations, while contemporary guidelines differ substantially in risk assessment, LDL-cholesterol targets, incorporation of risk enhancers, and use of coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring. Although recent guideline updates increasingly acknowledge South Asian ethnicity as a risk modifier, important gaps in calibration and implementation remain. Greater harmonisation of recommendations and validation of South Asian-specific risk assessment strategies are needed to improve cardiovascular prevention.

Article.ArticleTitle: Rural-Urban Disparities in Survival Among Patients With Malignant Primary Osseous Neoplasms of the Spine and Sacropelvis: A Population-Based Cohort Study.

Abstract.AbstractText: Background Malignant primary osseous neoplasms of the spine and sacropelvis are rare tumors whose outcomes rely heavily on specialized, guideline-driven care, which is concentrated in metropolitan referral centers. Investigations of rurality in this population have been limited by single-histology cohorts, small numbers of rural patients, and unadjusted comparisons, and none have weighed geographic disadvantage directly against the socioeconomic conditions with which it coexists. This study aimed to determine whether rural residence is independently associated with overall survival and cause-specific survival, and secondarily whether county-level median household income is independently associated with survival in the same models. Methodology This was a retrospective, population-based cohort study using the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database from 2000 to 2023. Patients with microscopically confirmed malignant chordoma, chondrosarcoma, osteosarcoma, or Ewing sarcoma of the vertebral column or the pelvic bones, sacrum, or coccyx with known survival time were included. Rurality was defined using SEER county attributes, with nonmetropolitan counties classified as rural. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models for overall survival and cause-specific survival were adjusted for demographic, socioeconomic, tumor, and treatment characteristics, with time-based interaction terms added where Schoenfeld residuals indicated violation of the proportional hazards assumption. Results Of 3,631 patients (median age = 51 years; 59% male), 3,255 (90%) resided in urban counties and 376 (10%) in rural counties. Rural residence was concentrated in low-income counties (54% below $60,000 vs. 4.1% of urban patients). Rurality was not independently associated with overall survival (hazard ratio (HR) = 0.95, 95% CI (confidence interval) = 0.82-1.09; p = 0.449) or cause-specific survival (HR = 0.94, 95% CI = 0.80-1.11; p = 0.457). County income showed a graded association with overall survival relative to counties below $60,000, with HRs of 0.82 ($80,000-$100,000), 0.72 ($100,000-$120,000), and 0.68 (>$120,000), all with p-values <0.001, and no difference for $60,000-$80,000 (HR = 1.01). A similar gradient was observed for cause-specific survival. Surgery was associated with lower mortality (overall survival: HR = 0.76; cause-specific survival: HR = 0.80; both p < 0.001), whereas radiotherapy was not. Unadjusted differences by rurality in stage at presentation and treatment receipt were small. Conclusions Rural residence conferred no independent survival disadvantage once socioeconomic and clinical factors were accounted for, whereas county-level income remained independently associated with mortality in a graded fashion. Because rural residence and low county income overlap heavily in this cohort, the survival signal appears to be carried by socioeconomic context rather than by geography. These tumors are rare, are not amenable to screening, and are largely managed at specialized referral centers, which may explain the absence of the rural disadvantage described for screen-detectable cancers. Identifying at-risk patients by geography alone may overlook socioeconomically disadvantaged patients in urban counties, and direct assessment of financial and access-related barriers may be more informative than rural-urban classification.

Article.ArticleTitle: Development of an evidence-based guideline for deprescribing potentially inappropriate medications in older adults.

Abstract.AbstractText: To develop an evidence-based guideline for deprescribing potentially inappropriate medications (PIMs) in older adults through systematic evidence synthesis and multidisciplinary expert consensus, providing a standardized framework to support deprescribing practice and pharmaceutical care.

Led by the Chinese Medical Association of Clinical Pharmacy and in collaboration with six National Clinical Research Centers for Geriatric Diseases, a multidisciplinary expert panel was established, encompassing geriatrics, clinical pharmacy, nursing, pharmaceutical administration, and pharmacoeconomics. On the basis of an evidence-based framework, a modified Delphi expert consultation method (two rounds) was employed to develop consensus statements. The evidence quality was evaluated via the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Evidence-Based Healthcare tools.

The integrated literature and opinions of Chinese experts led to a deprescribing management process. Named ORDER (includes five steps: organize the list, medication review, develop plan, execute plan, and realize feedback). In addition, we recommend the feasibility and priority of the PIM. This study provides practical recommendations for deprescribing PIM in older adults on the basis of 15 aspects.

The ORDER process represents China's first standardized protocol for deprescribing the management of PIM in older adults. Its multidisciplinary collaboration model and patient engagement mechanism provide a scalable pathway to improve rational medication use in geriatric care, offering significant clinical value for advancing comprehensive geriatric assessment systems.
